text:
As the first crisp autumn winds sweep across the East Sea, the port city of Pohang in North Gyeongsang Province begins producing "gwamegi" — Korea’s cherished winter delicacy of dried Pacific saury. But this season, a sharp slump in oceanic catches is turning the savory staple into a luxury commodity.
Pohang launched a nationwide promotional blitz on Wednesday at the National Assembly in Seoul, introducing the 2026–2027 season. Celebrated for its rich, chewy texture and deeply savory flavor, gwamegi is traditionally crafted in the seaside town of Guryongpo by hanging cleaned saury on wooden racks, allowing the freezing night temperatures and icy coastal winds to slowly dry and cure the fish over several weeks.
In Korean culinary culture, the delicacy holds a storied place as a nutrient-dense winter superfood. Packed with omega-3 fatty acids, the partially dried fish is prized for promoting cardiovascular health and circulation. It is typically served wrapped in fresh seaweed or perilla leaves, with spring onions and a dab of vinegar and chili sauce as condiments.
However, this year’s celebrations are being dampened by growing ecological and economic strain.
Dwindling Pacific saury catches have driven wholesale fish costs up nearly 40 percent compared to last year. Local producers have absorbed much of the burden to cushion retail buyers, but wholesale shipping prices have still risen roughly 20 percent.
"Our members have cut margins to the absolute minimum for consumers, but we face an unprecedented imbalance in raw supply," said Jang Chun-soo, head of the Pohang Guryongpo Gwamegi Industry Cooperative. Jang warned that unless global catch conditions improve, processing plants could be forced to end production early this winter.
To boost consumer interest despite rising costs, Pohang is rolling out a monthslong festival campaign. The annual Guryongpo Gwamegi Festival will run Saturday and Sunday at Ara Square in Guryongpo, followed by a pop-up tour across major transit hubs in the capital region, including Seoul Station on Nov. 16.
"Guryongpo gwamegi is a gift shaped by the clean East Sea and winter sea breezes," Pohang Mayor Pak Yong-son said. "Through strict quality control and food safety checks, we are ensuring consumers receive an authentic, healthy taste of winter."
